https://www.thetimes.com/article/labours.title: Labour’s Red Rev sacked for affairs
https://www.thetimes.com/article/labours.text:
A vicar who was selected as a Labour candidate at the last election but stood down when he was accused of sexual harassment has been sacked by the Church of England for adultery.
The Rev Steven Saxby, 49, who called himself the Red Rev, was nominated for the Cities of London and Westminster seat. He has now been removed from his role at St Barnabas Church in Walthamstow, east London.
In March last year Christine, his wife, said that she had discovered that he had an affair with an organist at the church in October 2018 and a four-year affair with an international pianist.
At the time she told the Daily Mail: “My husband of 20 years had an affair during October of last year, which I just found out about last night. Unfortunately, it was not the first. The ‘other woman’ accidentally revealed information which led me to finding out that he had an affair for four years with a trusted friend and sometime member of our congregation.”
Mrs Saxby, who was living with her husband and four children in the vicarage at the time, added: “I know that you will be shocked as I am about this. Please pray for us. We are in quite a precarious situation now regarding our house and future. I am trying so hard but it is difficult to remain dignified when your life is falling apart. I want to rage. The storm is still unfolding and every day brings more revelations. There seems to be no end to the lies.”
In March this year he was suspended by the Church of England. He apologised at the time for the “mistakes” he had made and any hurt caused.
Mr Saxby was to be Labour’s parliamentary candidate in the Cities of London and Westminster in February last year after he received support from the Unite union and the endorsement of John McDonnell, who was shadow chancellor of the exchequer. He also had the support of Jeremy Corbyn.
Critics questioned his suitability after a clip emerged of him speaking alongside George Galloway, the former MP, at a mosque in east London. Mr Saxby withdrew his candidacy after he was suspended by the Labour Party pending investigation of a complaint relating to sexual harassment. At the time he said that it was “a complaint I strongly refute”.
The central London seat, which includes the Houses of Parliament, was a key marginal at the election. It had been held by Mark Field, a Foreign Office minister who had been the Conservative MP since 2001. At the 2017 election his majority fell from 9,671 to 3,148 and he stood down last year after video emerged of him grabbing a Greenpeace activist during the chancellor’s Mansion House speech event. He said that he feared she was armed and later apologised. The police took no action.
At the election last year the Conservatives held the seat. Nickie Aiken beat Chuka Umunna, the former Labour minister who stood for the Lib Dems, into second place and Labour’s Gordon Nardell was third.
Last night a spokesman for the Diocese of Chelmsford said: “We hold everyone affected by this situation in our prayers.”
Mr Saxby was approached for comment.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Mark Carney on Brexit, the Bank of England and fighting climate change
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
In the spring of 2018, I was viewing the Picasso exhibition at the Tate Modern in London with Mark Carney, then governor of the Bank of England. We were in a group guided by a curator who stopped at an endless number of paintings to ask, “Can you see here the imagery representing Picasso’s penis?” To focus our attention, he gestured up and down with his hand. On the fifth or sixth occasion, the curator stopped by a big painting of a reclining woman in purples and pinks and asked again if we could see “the penis extending here, from the face and head”. At that moment I caught the governor’s eye and I corpsed. “Are you absolutely sure,” Carney deadpanned when we were released from the earnest tour, “that you could see the penises?”
You see, Mark Carney is funnier than you might have imagined if you’d just seen him on TV, talking about quantitative easing and banking regulation, those three lines across his brow appearing themselves to underscore the serious state of the UK’s economic health. Maybe you were concentrating on his analysis of the productivity gap, or maybe you were confused by just how unusually attractive he is for a central banker, what a well-cut blue suit he had on, what well-cut silver-flecked hair and what glorious mischief – in addition to the gravity, of course – that face brought to the television news.
The blue suit is on today, worn Macron-style with an open-neck white shirt, when I meet him at the BBC, where he is recording the first of his four Reith Lectures, to be broadcast in early December. The 55-year-old is now the UN secretary-general’s special envoy for climate action and finance, a role weaved into his lectures, which are about how to put values back into economic value.
There are two main thrusts: that in the West, governments have confused what is good for markets with what is good for society; and that both the banking crisis and the Covid crisis show why it is crucial to avert an “existential” climate crisis. “We don’t get a do-over on climate change; we’ll get a do-over on pandemics,” he tells me. “Unfortunately, there will be other viruses. And we’ll be better prepared.”
On his lapel is an eco-friendly poppy pin. On his wrist is a Swatch. I ask where the suit is from. “London. I don’t know,” he splutters. “I don’t like stuff like that.” Even when his chief of staff tries to encourage him – “But you’re so stylish, Mark” – he won’t say. So we’ll have to believe it was coincidence that his tie colour always brought out his grey-blue eyes. Mostly, he’s in a playful mood, teasing me as I ask him how he’s getting on these days. After all, he was in the global super-elite with an extraordinarily powerful job. “And now I’m living in Ottawa?” He laughs. “Thank you for looking out for my psychological welfare.” There were a few hiccups, he admits, not least the delayed arrival of his family’s worldly goods.
But look, he’s busy, busy, busy. Sure, Ottawa is a different pace, but Canada is still part of the G7. And no one feels quite settled in the pandemic, do they? “And from just always being on, and always…” he stalls. I think he wants to say “being in the public eye”.
“Canada is a very private place. There’s not the scrutiny that comes with the previous job,” he says. Do his two school-age girls – 14 and 16 – miss London, where they spent the past seven years? “Will they read this?” he asks himself. “Yes. So I think they like being back. I mean, everything is strange, right?”
He must be just a tiny bit relieved that he’s no longer responsible for stopping the country going bust. What about all the billions we owe? “Hahahaha,” he says. How dangerous is it? “Well, the first thing when looking at dangers is to look at the counterfactual, which is how dangerous would it be if the government weren’t taking these…” Perhaps he is uncomfortable talking about the Bank now, because halfway through the sentence he picks up my phone. “Oh, it’s a picture by Lucien Freud,” he says of the screensaver. It’s fantastic. Did you go to that exhibition at the Royal Academy? It was really good. Anyways.”
Yes, anyways. His life is different now. He gets up between 5.30 and 6am, laces his Adidas trainers, goes for a run. He runs through Ottawa’s wild spaces, through the light snow, along the river. Sometimes he has an earbud in for music or the news. Mostly he runs to think. If he kept going, he could be in Quebec – “That’s the way it feels” – but he circuits back towards home, ten kilometres under his belt. The energy in his house is green, so his hot shower expends zero emissions, he can shave under zero-emission lightbulbs and sit down at a computer powered by the sun, his toes warmed by zero-emission heating. (In his own small way, Carney is pretty much at net zero.)
There are Zooms with Boris Johnson in his capacity as finance adviser for COP26, the UN Climate Change Conference (a job for which he is paid a symbolic $1), as well as more “private chats” with Johnson and Canada’s prime minister, Justin Trudeau, where he dispenses advice about the Covid pandemic. There are on-screen meetings with his fellow trustees on the board of the World Economic Forum, and for his one properly paid role at the asset manager Brookfield.
Also, he’s been writing a book: Value(s): Building a Better World For All. “The dreaded book,” he groans. “I went up Kilimanjaro once, and I vowed to tell everyone afterwards, ‘Just, you know, don’t go up Kilimanjaro. It was really difficult.’ So I feel duty bound to say, ‘If you’re anything like me, don’t write a book. It’s really difficult.’ ”
It’s safe to say he isn’t actually afraid of anything “really difficult”. After all, he took the role as governor of the Bank of England (2013-2020) because, as he phrases it to me today with a wink, “I like a challenge.” And despite his protests, I can’t help but think that none of what he is doing today is challenge enough for Carney. Colleagues say he has a phenomenal work ethic, is incredibly, ruthlessly focused – and expects a similar pace and intensity from those around him. (He tended to hire from a specific pool: people trained at Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan or Morgan Stanley, with SAS-like endurance skills.) So I ask about that other big challenge: does he still have ambitions to be prime minister of Canada?
“When did I…?” He laughs. “Whose idea was it to ask that, Charlotte?” Didn’t we all think he wanted to be prime minister of Canada one day? And then instead of saying something about how brilliant Justin Trudeau is, or even – perhaps – that he just wants to concentrate his efforts on solving the climate crisis, he just sits and looks at me, lips pressed shut yet grinning. OK, I say. You’re not going to answer that.
Another question he won’t answer is, “Are you annoyed that you didn’t get a peerage from the British government?” He is one of only a handful in the Bank’s 121-governor history not to walk away with a gong. And arguably until now – because current incumbent Andrew Bailey certainly has his hands full – he steered the Bank through one of the worst of times.
And look, he gave us a lot. He weathered the batshit wars over Brexit and the briefings against him for refusing to endorse sunlit uplands. He was criticised by anti-expert government ministers, bore a tidal wave of grief against global elites (of which he – a former Goldman, Davos-attending G7 supremo – was probably the finest example ever fashioned). Even today, the fallout reverberates: he’s coy on mundane family matters, such as where his two older daughters attend university, “Because you know there are nasty people who use it.”
Ah, the “nasty people”. After the Brexit vote in 2016, there really were people who hated Mark Carney. And not just Jacob Rees-Mogg, who demanded he resign for suggesting that leaving the EU might trigger a recession, or Iain Duncan Smith, who warned him, mafia-like, to be “very careful” with his choice of words. They loathed him for telling Boris Johnson that life outside the EU may not be “a land of cake and consumption”. They thought not that it was his job to assess risk, but that he was a Canadian upstart, a Remoaner sympathiser, the “architect of Project Fear”. A mark of how insane the world was: in an interview on Newsnight, two members of the public said that Carney – with his economics doctorate, 13 years in investment banking and years overseeing two G7 central banks – “doesn’t know any more than we do really, does he?”
Although he is an expert diplomat, “frosty” is a word used by observers to describe his relationship with Theresa May. They believe he found it profoundly unhelpful that May was at loggerheads with her chancellor, Philip Hammond, at such a critical time for the UK economy. When I ask if he got on with Theresa May, he replies with a high-pitched, “Yep.” I relay an anecdote about him being made to sit away from her on a government plane flying to Hangzhou for the G20 in 2016. He says, “How long is this interview? Is it like a month?” He remains unbowed on his view that Brexit is bad for Britain today. When I ask if he can be honest now about just how bad, “I was honest all along. I was straight up all along. It hasn’t changed.”
For a while, everyone seemed to forget that Carney was hired to save us. His arrival was fêted: the George Clooney of governors he was called (“a low bar” was his reply); “a rock star of central bankers”. “I mean, OK,” he says now. “But you wouldn’t want to be at that concert, the central bankers’ Glastonbury.”
In 2012, the chancellor, George Osborne, spent most of the year chasing Carney around the planet, beseeching him to be our governor. Carney said no. He said, “No, and never.” Can he describe how Osborne finally seduced him in Mexico City during the G20 finance ministers’ meeting? He says Osborne got him up to his room at the Nikko hotel, which was “very small”, and they had breakfast – fruit, because Osborne was in his extreme 5:2 diet phase. “I did warn him at one stage. I was like, ‘George, it’s 5:2, not 2:5. You are supposed to eat some of these days.’ He was very thin there for a while.” Osborne agreed to reduce the governor’s term from eight years to five so that Carney could factor in the needs of his family, and to up the salary from that of his predecessor, Mervyn King, in lieu of a pension. Is that what swung it?
“His persistence certainly helped,” says Carney. But also “the nature of the challenge. At the time, I was going to where the challenges were the greatest.” The Bank was in semi-disgrace after failing to warn of the black cloud on the horizon before the financial crisis. Carney puts it bluntly, “We had a financial sector that had failed. There’s no polite way of saying it.”
So, he publicly backtracked on “no, and never” with a nice-touch line about having learnt from James Bond to “never say never”. He arrived and helped ward off a triple-dip recession. It strikes him as odd, now, that one of his worries had been that he’d be a “foreigner” – “Should’ve been the least thing I was concerned about.” He set out to win hearts and minds. He ran the London Marathon, winked at the BBC economics editor in a live press conference, teased politicians (Labour’s Pat McFadden likened him to “an unreliable boyfriend”). He took off his suit and put on shorts for the Wilderness festival (held at Cornbury Park, owned by his brother-in-law at the time, Lord Rotherwick). And there was Wimbledon in 2016, which produced probably the most Mark Carney-ish still of all time: Jude Law wearing an expression like the WTF emoji, while his girlfriend moos at Carney’s every word.
And he didn’t behave like a flash banker. He lived in West Hampstead as opposed to, say, Regent’s Park or Mayfair, spending a fraction of his housing allowance. He wasn’t above bantz, especially with Osborne – one male friend describes him as “tickly”.
And nor was his British wife, Diana Fox Carney, the kind of person with a Net-A-Porter van parked outside the house. She didn’t do blow-dries or heels or manicures (“I’m not a make-up person”). She’s as clever as her husband, with a first in PPE, one master’s in agricultural economics, another in international relations, and every bit as doesn’t-suffer-fools, although possibly she makes less effort to hide it. Her own father’s description is that she’s an “eco warrior”. Friends say she worries about the future of the planet. “She thinks about climate change as in, ‘What does it mean for my family? How are we going to get through this crisis? What little can we do to make sure that the world’s a better place?’ She’s a worrier and campaigner.”
For a while in London she ran a blog, Eco Products That Work, which described teabags as a “pet hate” – “Do we really need an extra 40cm2 of bleached and printed paper with every cup of tea?”– railed against plastic-covered lever arch files, offered alternative treatments for headlice and plant pots made of fired cow dung. She was a fan of the book The Spirit Level. But she “hated” the mocking of tabloids, who’d describe her disparagingly as an anti-capitalist, leftist, a “posh hippy” who wore baking powder-based deodorant and £10 vegan shoes. She’d answer the door to journalists with a curt, “Hello, I’m not talking,” and her Twitter feed was locked.
At the Picasso exhibition she was as unreadable as marble. But I once saw her on a walk with her parents along a canal in north London and she was relaxed and laughing and almost unrecognisable. She and Carney met in the Nineties as postgrads through the Oxford University ice hockey club, a sport they both loved. Joceyln Taguchi, who was on the same team, says Diana was “our strongest player”, a skilled skater and shooter. Carney was the men’s team’s goalie, as he had been at Harvard, where he was on the subs bench. In his one full game he saved every shot, but it wasn’t enough to win him a full-time spot. His coach at Harvard, Bill Cleary, later said that it was always the bench-warmers who did well in life. “Over the years, guys like him are the ones who have become successful. The guys with the ability sometimes have too much – they don’t know what it is to work.”
Carney was born in Fort Smith, in the freezing Northwest Territories, the middle of three sons and a daughter. His father, Bob, was a head teacher and later a history professor, and he grew up in a house full of books. His mother, Verlie, gave up teaching and kept them warm. “If my mother was making porridge when I came upstairs it was a bad, bad sign. It meant it was really cold outside – minus 30.” When he was small, they moved to Edmonton – known locally as Deadmonton – and he was enrolled at the Jesuit-run St Francis Xavier High School. His chemistry teacher said he always had a smile on his face. He had a paper round and shovelled snow for pocket money. At Harvard he was remembered for “counting the pennies”, returning home in summer to work as a garden landscaper at a hospital. He chose Goldman Sachs over academia primarily to pay off his student debt. His Harvard roommate, Peter Chiarelli, later said, “Carney is Canadian, through and through. He left Wall Street, where he was making oodles of money, because even back in university he wanted to make his mark in public service.”
In person he does that North American thing of referring to people by their full titles: Prime Minister Cameron, Secretary of State Sharma. But he also uses slang, “like”, and that uptick rhetorical “right?”. And then there’s the jargon. “I’ll speak like an economist now,” he says at one point, and sentences land like spaghetti. He adds, “Hopefully you’re gonna make all this sound coherent.”
It’s said that he put an electric shock through the sleepy Bank of Canada when he arrived in 2007, aged 42. The Goldman training meant he worked through the night, even weekends. “Yeah, well, we did have a financial crisis,” he shrugs. But he allows for the possibility that he did good. “Two things: one, the world almost blew up; second, Canada didn’t. I don’t know if there’s a connection between the two.”
At some point Carney, like his wife, became preoccupied by climate change. He joked privately that he’d become a committed “tree-hugger”, but when I use the word he’s prickly over whether I mean literally or metaphorically (God, his defensiveness is frustrating). He says, “For a long period, I expected this problem to be dealt with decisively by those who had the responsibility.” By which he means politicians. And big polluting companies who don’t clean up after themselves. He says it’s partly “the nature of governments” to dither, but it’s clearly something that literally – and not metaphorically – pisses him off. He thought for a long time, “OK, well, they won’t let this happen. This will be taken care of.” With growing panic that turned into, “Hang on, is it being taken care of?” Now he’s the one taking decisive action. “Complacency is really the enemy of finance,” he used to say. Now it’s the enemy of the planet.
One point he makes: sectors in finance – insurance, for instance – see the black clouds rolling in precisely because it’s their job to prepare, price and manage risk. “The most sophisticated managers of this physical climate risk are based at Lloyd’s of London and the UK property and casualty insurance industry,” he says. At the Bank of England they realised, “ ‘Well, it’s not just the physical risk, it’s the change to the value of virtually every financial asset in the future.’ ” That means having a higher carbon price, moving to renewable power, and re-evaluating the price of everything. Some commodities – oil – are not going to be as valuable. “Three quarters of coal cannot be burnt; half of natural gas; a third of oil. We need to recognise that those truly are stranded assets.”
A White House under Donald Trump has been a huge challenge for climate issues. I ask if he has met the president or the first lady, and he twinkles and asks if I mean in “a social sense”. Well, yes. “I have met him at a few of the G20 summits.” Anything he’d like to share? He shakes his head laughing, waving his arms like an aircraft marshal. What a tease. He has not met Joe Biden, but welcomes his views. “It is always good not to deny an existential risk. That’s a good place to start. [Biden has a] very thoughtful and comprehensive approach to these issues. The US will be critical to a speedy resolution on climate change.”
I ask what he thinks of Extinction Rebellion and he pauses, and then gives a halting answer about the importance of social movements but also a respect for democracy and freedom of speech. “I think Fridays for Future has been more influential than Extinction Rebellion,” he concludes. He uses the prompt to talk about the “legislated objective for net zero” – ie it is enshrined in British law that companies must have a net-zero target for carbon dioxide by 2050 (with a push to do it before). Carney asks the heads of financial institutions, “So, what’s your plan?” He says generally there are three responses. First, yes, I have a plan. Second, I can’t, so I will “run my business off”. Both of these are “totally valid options”. The third is the arrogant, “I’m a company apart from society. I don’t care that’s a law of the land. I don’t have a plan, and I don’t intend to have a plan.” He says of that attitude, “Well, good luck raising capital.”The Reith Lectures given by Mark Carney are on BBC Radio 4 and BBC Sounds from December 2Exclusive subscriber offerSubscribers can pre-order Mark Carney’s new book, Value(s): Building a Better World for All, published by HarperCollins on March 18, 2021, and save £9 on the £30 RRP. https://www.thetimes.com/article/extinct.title: Extinction Rebellion hangs protest wreath on Cenotaph
https://www.thetimes.com/article/extinct.text:
Extinction Rebellion activists placed a protest wreath declaring climate change a “war” on the Cenotaph, hours before the Prince of Wales and Duchess of Cornwall attended the Westminster Abbey service for Remembrance Day.
The environmental campaign group hung a banner that read “Honour their sacrifice, climate change means war” and a wreath of poppies bearing a slogan on the memorial this morning.
After the banner had been placed, Donald Bell, a British Army veteran and member of Extinction Rebellion, observed two minutes’ silence before hanging the wreath. Police officers later removed it before the service.
Mr Bell, 64, who was injured in a car bomb in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, said he wanted to warn the public about the global climate crisis and how it may lead to more armed conflicts.
“I took action today knowing that I would be criticised,” he said. “I knew that I would be accused of being disrespectful and hated by many for speaking out in this way. Remembrance Day is never an easy time for veterans and this was not an easy decision for me to make.
“This government’s own climate advisers, the Committee on Climate Change, said last year that they have a Dad's Army approach to protecting British people from the impacts of climate change.
“Their report in June this year showed that the government has failed to meet all but two of the 31 milestones it set itself for reducing emissions. This government is criminally negligent and young people today will pay the price for their failure.”
The public were asked not to gather at the Cenotaph due to coronavirus restrictions, and instead were encouraged to pause on their doorsteps or by windows for the traditional two minutes’ silence at 11am.
A televised service was held at Westminster Abbey to mark the centenary of the burial of the Unknown Warrior. Simon Armitage, the poet laureate, read his poem The Bed, a tribute written for the centenary, during the service.
The poem charts how the fallen soldier is transported from being “broken and sleeping rough in a dirt grave” to being buried “among drowsing poets and dozing saints” in Westminster Abbey.
The Bed by Simon ArmitageSharp winds scissor and scythe those plains.And because you are broken and sleeping roughin a dirt grave, we exchange the crude wooden crossfor the hilt and blade of a proven sword;to hack through the knotted dark of the next world,yes, but to lean on as well at a stile or gatelooking out over fens or wealds or fells or wolds. That sword, drawn from a king’s sheath,fits a commoner’s hand, and is yours to keep.
And because frost plucks at the threadsof your nerves, and your bones stew in the rain,bedclothes of zinc and oak are trimmedand tailored to fit. Sandbags are drafted in,for bolstering limbs and pillowing dreams,and we throw in a fistful of battlefield soil:an inch of the earth, your share of the spoils.
The heavy sheet of stone is Belgian marblebuffed to a high black gloss, the blanketa flag that served as an altar cloth. Darknessfiles past, through until morning, its head bowed.Molten bullets embroider incised words.Among drowsing poets and dozing saintsthe tall white candles are vigilant sentriespresenting arms with stiff yellow flames;so nobody treads on the counterpane,but tiptoeing royal brides in satin slipperswill dress and crown you with luminous flowers.
All this for a soulwithout name or rank or age or home, because youare the son we lost, and your rest is ours.
Unknown Warrior 100, the service from Westminster Abbey, will be available on BBC iPlayer.
